To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the two cloud screening methods developed for the OCO- 2 mission, the Iterative Maximum A Posteriori (IMAP) Differential Optical Absoption Spectroscopy (DOAS) Preprocessor and the A-Band Preprocesor (ABP), have been shown to be capable of identifying clouds with high accuracy and precision.

(1) the cloud screening algorithms used by OCO-2 are able to identify clouds with an accuracy of  ≈ 85 % when compared to MODIS observations, (2) the cloud screen algorithms are able to identify high clouds with an accuracy better than 90 %, and (3) the cloud-screening algorithms have some difficulty in identifying low clouds and near-surface clouds.
the OCO-1 and OCO-2 algorithms are able to identify cloud and aerosol contaminated observations in the OCO-3 data set with an accuracy of 85 %.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the validation of the cloud screening algorithm used in the OCO-1 and OCO-2 missions.
the validation of the cloud screening methods used by the Orbiting Carbon Observatory (OCO-1) and OCO-2.
the development and evaluation of cloud screening algorithms for the Orbiting Carbon Observatory (OCO) satellite instrument.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cloud screening algorithms are performing well and that the OCO-3 algorithm should be able to screen  ≃ 25 % of all soundings, with a cloud screening success rate of  ≈ 85 % and a failure rate of  ≤ 15 %.
the OCO-1 and OCO-2 algorithms have performed as expected, with some minor improvements in the OCO-3 cloud screening algorithm.
the OCO-1 and OCO-2 algorithms are robust and perform very well in identifying the majority of the cloud-contaminated measurements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the OCO-3 cloud screening algorithms are robust and reliable, and the results are consistent with the MODIS cloud screening algorithms.
OCO-2's cloud screening algorithms perform well, and that the algorithms can be tuned to achieve a high level of agreement ( ≃  85 %) with collocated MODIS cloud screening products.
OCO-2 is able to detect clouds with an efficiency of about 85 % with a false detection rate of  ≈ 15 %.
The main takeaway from our work is that
OCO-2 is capable of screening for cloud and aerosol contamination in its measurements with an accuracy that is comparable to other satellite missions.

the OCO-1 cloud screening algorithms are performing as expected and that, with the appropriate algorithmic tuning, the cloud screening algorithms can be used to process  ≃ 20–25 % ( ≃ 50 %) of the OCO2 data set with an estimated cloud screening success rate of 85 % (75 %).
the OCO-3 and OCO-4 missions will benefit from a robust cloud screening algorithm that will allow for the retrieval of high-quality CO2 column abundance estimates.
